title: Say which AI wrote it: AI transparency for Open Source projects
content:
Say which AI wrote it
A simple practice for Open Source projects that accept contributions written with AI tools. Each commit names the model that wrote it, and a person answers for the change. Nothing more is needed to start: one line at the end of a commit, and a few sentences in the files a project already has.
The practice, in three sentences
Say so
A commit that was not written by a human ends with a trailer naming the model and its version.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
A human answers for it
Every change is read, understood and tested by the person who submits it, whoever or whatever wrote it. An agent does not open a pull request on its own.
No shame, no ranking
Declaring an AI tool is never held against a contribution. Nobody has to use one, and nobody has to explain why they do not.
What a project adds
The shortest way is one paragraph in CONTRIBUTING.md. The whole practice is a section in three files, ready to copy:
- CONTRIBUTING.md, for people;
- AGENTS.md, for AI agents, which then write the trailer themselves;
- two boxes in the pull request template.
The same commitments exist as a short, versioned text, the AI transparency charter, that a project can adopt by name.
What it looks like in real projects
This site follows a few projects as examples. For each one it reads the commits and the pull requests, and shows what their contributors declare: which models are named, since when, and by how many people. The figures are a lower bound, and the pages rank nobody.
All the projects · Statistics, all projects together
The list is a showcase, not a registry: it is kept short on purpose. To see the same pages for your own projects, run the tool yourself.
Run it for your own projects
The tool that builds these pages is free software, written in Python with the standard library only. It reads a list of repositories and writes a static site, which any web server can publish.
pip install git+https://github.com/cedricbonhomme/ai-disclosure
ai-disclosure build        # reads projects/, writes _site/
One small file per project says where the repository is and from which date its rule applies. The README explains the rest.
Not every project chooses this
Some projects refuse AI-generated contributions, others set no rule. This site takes no side on whether to use AI: it describes one way to be open about it. How other projects do it is compared on its own page.

report.summary: A lightweight open-source convention asks contributors to name the AI model in a commit trailer, with a human accountable for every change.
report.background: AI coding assistants now write a substantial share of code, including in open source, but projects have wildly different rules: some ban AI-generated contributions outright, others say nothing, and a few require disclosure. Maintainers need to know provenance for licensing, security review, and accountability, yet heavy verification is impractical for volunteer projects. Commit trailers already exist for co-authors and sign-offs, so a lightweight convention can piggyback on git. The Say Which AI initiative proposes a voluntary, non-punitive standard: disclose the model, keep a human responsible, and avoid ranking contributors by AI use. It arrives as agentic coding tools and AGENTS.md files make machine-authored patches more common.
key_points: The convention has three parts: any commit not written by a human ends with a trailer such as 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5', a person must read, understand and test every change they submit, and declaring AI use is never penalized. Agents cannot open pull requests on their own.

Adoption is deliberately low-effort. A project adds a paragraph to CONTRIBUTING.md, a section to AGENTS.md so agents write the trailer themselves, and two checkboxes in its pull request template. A short versioned 'AI transparency charter' can also be adopted by name.

The website showcases a curated set of projects, parsing commits and pull requests to show which models are declared, since when, and by how many contributors. It presents figures as a lower bound and explicitly ranks no one, keeping the focus on transparency rather than surveillance.

The underlying ai-disclosure tool is free Python software using only the standard library. It reads a list of repositories and generates a static site, so any project can reproduce the same transparency pages. One small config file per project sets the repository and the date its disclosure rule started.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a small but concrete step toward provenance norms: model names and versions become part of the software supply chain record, alongside licenses and signed-off-by lines. For developers, it lowers the cost of disclosure and reinforces human accountability without banning assistants or shaming users. For regular users, it improves trust in open-source projects that increasingly contain machine-written code. The limits are real: compliance is voluntary, trailers can be omitted or spoofed, and 'AI-written' is hard to define at the boundary of autocomplete and autonomous agents. It works best as a cultural norm, not a technical enforcement mechanism.
report.tools: Follow ai-disclosure (github.com/cedricbonhomme/ai-disclosure) to generate disclosure pages for your repositories; read the Say Which AI site's copy-ready CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md, and PR template sections. Watch the emerging AGENTS.md convention for instructing coding agents, git commit trailers as a lightweight metadata channel, and the AI transparency charter for a reusable policy text. Projects that want stricter controls may also compare bans and gated-review policies documented on the site.
